## Section 4. Program Design & Activities (~800 words)

---

**Theory of change.** [Organization]'s Evening Literacy Initiative rests on a simple, evidence-based premise: when K–3 students who are reading below grade level receive frequent, structured, one-on-one decoding and comprehension instruction from trained tutors — delivered in their neighborhoods, in their home languages, and on schedules their families can actually use — they close measurable reading gaps within a school year, and those gains translate into improved third-grade reading proficiency, reduced grade retention, and stronger long-term academic trajectories. Our activities (intensive tutoring, family literacy engagement, and teacher coordination) directly address the three barriers named in the Need section: insufficient one-on-one instructional time in school, lack of evening and in-language services, and weak links between school-day instruction and out-of-school support. Short-term outcomes (improved decoding fluency, increased reading minutes at home, stronger teacher-tutor alignment) feed directly into mid-term outcomes (grade-level reading by end of program year) and long-term outcomes (third-grade reading proficiency, reduced K–12 service costs). [ATTACH: 1-page logic model as Attachment A.]
*Rubric: Program Design — logic; link to Need.*

**Participant pathway.** Each year, 240 students will move through the program in two cohorts of 120, with each cohort running for an academic semester (18 weeks). Intake (weeks 1–2) includes teacher referral, family enrollment meeting in the family's preferred language, baseline reading assessment using [ASSESSMENT TOOL], and a goal-setting conversation with parent, tutor, and classroom teacher. Services (weeks 3–16) consist of the three core activities described below, delivered concurrently. Exit (weeks 17–18) includes post-assessment, a family celebration and progress conference, and a warm handoff to the classroom teacher with a written summary of gains and recommended next steps. Follow-up occurs at 3 and 6 months post-exit through brief teacher check-ins and a family survey, with re-enrollment offered to any student still below grade level.
*Rubric: Program Design — participant pathway; dosage; cohort structure.*

**Activity 1: Intensive one-on-one tutoring.** Each enrolled student receives two 45-minute tutoring sessions per week for 14 weeks (28 sessions, 21 hours total per participant), delivered by trained tutors using a structured literacy curriculum grounded in the science of reading [CURRICULUM NAME, PUBLISHER]. Sessions take place at partner sites in [NEIGHBORHOOD A] and [NEIGHBORHOOD B] — [PARTNER SITE 1], [PARTNER SITE 2], and [PARTNER SITE 3] — from 5:00 to 8:00 p.m. weekdays and 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. Saturdays. Tutors are paid, trained paraprofessionals supervised by a credentialed reading specialist; at least [X]% of tutors are bilingual in [LANGUAGES], and all complete [NUMBER] hours of pre-service training plus weekly coaching. **This activity directly addresses the barrier identified by T. Nguyen and [X]% of surveyed teachers: students need daily one-on-one decoding work that the school day cannot provide.** [MOU: Attach site-use agreements with partner sites as Attachment B.]
*Rubric: Program Design — activity detail; staffing; equity (language, schedule, neighborhood); link to Need.*

**Activity 2: Family literacy engagement.** Each family participates in one 60-minute family literacy session per month (4 sessions per semester) and receives a weekly take-home reading packet matched to their child's level and available in [LANGUAGES]. Sessions are offered in two formats — in-person at partner sites with childcare and a light meal provided, and virtually with tech support — and are facilitated by bilingual family engagement staff. Content covers home reading routines, how to support decoding and comprehension at home, and navigating school communication. **This activity directly addresses the barrier Maria G. named: working parents need literacy support that fits evening and weekend schedules and arrives in their home language.**
*Rubric: Program Design — activity detail; equity (language, childcare, format); link to Need/community voice.*

**Activity 3: Teacher-tutor coordination.** For each enrolled student, the assigned tutor and classroom teacher complete a structured 15-minute coordination call every three weeks (6 calls per semester) using a shared digital progress log. The reading specialist facilitates a monthly 45-minute cross-site case conference with partner-school literacy staff. This activity ensures that tutoring reinforces, rather than runs parallel to, school-day instruction — directly addressing the alignment gap identified in [LOCAL EDUCATION COALITION REPORT, YEAR].
*Rubric: Program Design — activity detail; alignment with existing systems.*

**Evidence base.** The program design draws on three converging evidence sources: (1) meta-analyses of high-dosage tutoring showing average effects of 0.37 standard deviations on literacy outcomes for K–3 students when delivered at least three times per week by trained tutors [Nickow, Oreopoulos & Quan, 2020]; (2) structured literacy approaches grounded in the science of reading, which show particularly strong effects for English learners and students with early reading difficulties [SOURCE, YEAR]; and (3) [Organization]'s own [YEAR] pilot with [NUMBER] students at [PARTNER SCHOOL], in which [X]% of participants moved up at least one reading level over a single semester [Internal Evaluation, YEAR].
*Rubric: Program Design — evidence base; local pilot.*

**Equity practices embedded in the design.** Beyond the language, schedule, and neighborhood decisions above, the program provides round-trip transportation vouchers or rides for any family that requests them, offers on-site childcare for siblings during family sessions, pays tutors a living wage of $[X]/hour to support recruitment from the target neighborhoods themselves, and uses a sliding-scale materials fee that is $0 for all income-eligible families.
